column2: Hi there. Today's question is on pensions and inheritance tax.
How much of your pension will be taxed when you die?
How can you reduce the bill?
And what's the catch?
I'm Steve Hunt.
I'm a Chartered Insurance Risk Manager and a Trust and Estate Practitioner.
And I've been in the industry since 1980.
And I answer the questions that you ask.
Today's question is an important one because there is a time limit on it,
because the people who will be most affected by this
are estates and families where the main member
will die before April 2027.
The short answer.
How much of your pension is taxed when you die depends on two things: when you die, and how old you are.
From 6 April 2027, in the UK, most pensions you have not spent count as part of your estate for inheritance tax when you die.
If you die at 75 or over, your family also pays income tax on what they draw out.
In our made-up example, with real numbers for the 2026/27 tax year, a £500,000 pension ends up costing one family £516,000 in tax.
That is 103% of the pension.
And one name on a form, filled in before 6 April 2027, could have made it nought.
Will my pension count for inheritance tax when I die?
If you die on or after 6 April 2027, most pensions you have not spent count in your estate for inheritance tax.
Yes.
That includes money in drawdown that you have not taken out.
The Finance Act 2026 added section 150A to the Inheritance Tax Act 1984.
It treats the money left in your pension as part of your estate when you die.
The law calls it notional pension property.
Before 6 April 2027, most pensions where the trustees decide who is paid sit outside your estate.
From that date, they are in.
There are a few exceptions, such as death in service lump sums and some pensions paid to dependants.
This is about personal and workplace pension pots.
The State Pension works differently.
If your pension goes to your husband, wife, civil partner or a charity, it is normally free of inheritance tax, under sections 18 and 23.
Inheritance tax may then be due when the second of you dies.
HMRC estimates that in the 2027/28 tax year about 10,500 estates will pay inheritance tax where before they would not have, and about 38,500 more will pay a bigger bill.
That is 49,000 estates in the first year.
How much inheritance tax will my pension pay?
Your pension pays its share of the whole estate's tax bill, in proportion to its value.
Section 265 of the Inheritance Tax Act 1984 shares the tax out between everything in the estate, by value.
I call this the sharing rule.
If your pension is one fifth of your estate, it pays one fifth of the bill.
HMRC's Technical Note 2, published on 27 August 2026, says the same: the tax on the whole estate is shared out between its different parts.
Your executors work out the pension's share.
They, or your family, can ask the pension provider to pay it straight from the pension, using a payment notice under section 226B.
The provider must pay within 35 days, and only if the pension's share is £1,000 or more.
Will my family pay income tax on my pension as well?
Yes, if you die at 75 or over.
Your family pays income tax, at their own rate, on what they draw.
Under section 579CZA of the Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003, money drawn from an inherited pension is tax free if the person it came from died under 75.
If they died at 75 or over, every pound drawn counts as the family member's own taxable income.
There used to be a two-year time limit to keep this tax free.
At the Budget on 28 October 2026, the government said it is removing it for payments made from that date.
The law to do this is still to come.
The inheritance tax paid out of the pension is not taxed again as income.
How can the tax on a pension come to more than 100%?
Meet the Miggins family.
They are made up.
Their numbers are real, using 2026/27 rates and allowances, with no growth.
Mr Miggins is 70 and seriously ill.
He has a personal pension of £500,000 that he has never touched.
His expression of wish form is the form that tells the trustees who he would like his pension to go to.
It says one word.
Their daughter Amy is 45.
Wife.
She works at a bank and earns £100,000 a year.
Mr Miggins dies in January 2027, aged 71.
The trustees pay his pension into a pension in Mrs Miggins' name.
There is no inheritance tax, because he died before 6 April 2027.
There is no income tax, because he died under 75.
Mrs Miggins does not need the money, so she leaves it in the pension.
Mrs Miggins dies in 2029, aged 76.
Now two things have changed.
First, her inherited pension counts in her estate, because she died after 6 April 2027.
HMRC's Technical Note 2 confirms this, even though her husband died before that date.
Second, she died over 75.
So Amy pays income tax on every pound she draws.
What does the Miggins family actually pay?
The Miggins family pays £516,000 in tax on a £500,000 pension: £300,000 of extra inheritance tax and £216,000 of income tax.
Mrs Miggins' other estate is £2 million, most of it the house.
The house goes to Amy, and Amy lives in England, not Scotland.
Mrs Miggins has her own allowances and her husband's.
That is £650,000 of nil rate band, and £350,000 of residence nil rate band, the extra allowance for passing a home to children.
£1 million in all.
Without the pension, the inheritance tax is 40% of £1 million.
That is £400,000.
With the pension, her estate is £2.5 million.
Above £2 million, the residence nil rate band is cut by £1 for every £2, under section 8D.
She loses £250,000 of it.
Her allowances fall to £750,000.
The tax is 40% of £1.75 million.
That is £700,000.
So the pension has added £300,000 to the bill.
But under the sharing rule, the pension is one fifth of the estate, so it pays one fifth of the £700,000.
That is £140,000.
The rest of the estate, the house money, pays the rest.
Its bill goes up from £400,000 to £560,000.
That leaves £360,000 in the pension for Amy.
Amy earns £100,000.
She draws £24,000 a year for 15 years, which takes her income to £124,000 each year.
Between £100,000 and £125,140, she loses £1 of her personal allowance for every £2 of extra income, under section 35 of the Income Tax Act 2007.
So every pound she draws is taxed at an effective 60%.
Add it up.
£300,000 of extra inheritance tax, plus £216,000 of income tax.
That is £516,000.
On a £500,000 pension, that is 103%.
The family hands over every pound Dad saved, and threepence on top.
Put another way, the family ends up £16,000 worse off than if Dad had never saved a penny into the pension.
The 103% compares the family's extra tax with the size of the pension.
No single tax is charged at 103%.
Why is it 103% and not the 67% in the papers?
It is 103% because three things work together: the £2 million taper, Amy's 60% rate, and the sharing rule.
Most headlines take 40% inheritance tax off the pension, then 45% income tax off the 60% that is left.
That is how they get 67%.
Here, the pension added £300,000 to the bill but paid only £140,000.
The other £160,000 came from the house money.
So £160,000 more was left in the pension, and Amy pays 60% on that too.
That is £96,000 more income tax.
The inheritance tax is £700,000 either way.
If the pension had paid the full £300,000 it added, only £200,000 would be left.
Amy's income tax would be £120,000.
The total would be £420,000, or 84%.
The sharing rule is what takes it over 100%.
Can one name on my expression of wish form change this?
Yes, if you die before 6 April 2027 and under 75.
Naming your children on the form lets the trustees pay them a pension free of both taxes.
Under the Finance Act 2004, Schedule 28, paragraph 27A, while your wife is alive the trustees can only pay your grown-up children a pension if you named them on the form.
Suppose that a month before he died, Mr Miggins had asked for a new form and added one line.
Amy, daughter, 10%.
The trustees could then pay the pension straight to Amy, as a pension in her own name.
The trustees still decide.
But now Amy is on the form, and Mrs Miggins has told them she does not need the money.
Inheritance tax: nought.
He died before 6 April 2027.
Income tax: nought.
He died under 75.
Inheritance tax on the pension when Mum dies: nought.
It was never hers.
Nought, or 103%.
One form.
Changing the form is not a gift for inheritance tax, as long as the form does not bind the trustees and they keep the final say.
HMRC's Inheritance Tax Manual, at IHTM17052 and IHTM17071, says there is no lifetime transfer.
What's the catch?
There are six.
One.
The nought needs Dad to die before 6 April 2027 and under 75.
From 6 April 2027, a pension paid to a child counts in Dad's own estate for inheritance tax.
Only the part paid to a husband, wife, civil partner or charity is exempt.
Two.
The trustees decide.
Naming Amy makes her eligible.
It does not guarantee she is paid.
Three.
Not every pension offers a pension to a named child.
Many modern personal pensions do.
Some older plans only pay a lump sum.
Without the name, the trustees could still choose to pay Amy a lump sum, but the name keeps the option of a pension in her name.
Four.
If the children are paid, the husband or wife may get less.
Think about everyone's needs.
Five.
Whatever Amy still has in the pension when she dies counts in her own estate.
Six.
The 103% depends on the numbers: a £2 million estate with a home in it, full allowances, Amy on £100,000 for 15 years, today's tax bands and no growth.
Scottish income tax rates are different.
What can I check today?
Check who is named on your expression of wish form, for every pension you have.
Ask your pension provider for a copy of your form.
Ask if they can pay your children a pension in their own name, not just a lump sum, and how to add them.
Being named is the point.
Some providers let you name children without a percentage.
Others need the percentages to add up to 100%.
Follow your provider's form.
The full transcript, with every source, is on inheritancetaxexplained.co.uk.
Tax rules can change, and how they apply depends on your own circumstances.
This is education only.
It is not advice. ---
And as always, I leave you with those immortal words from Roy Jenkins,
probably truer now than when he first spoke them
in 1986 in the House of Commons
when he was talking about inheritance tax,
where he said it was a voluntary levy,
paid by those who distrust their heirs
more than they dislike the Inland Revenue.
And my next question that I will answer for you
will be on nominees' annuities.
What are they, and how can they be used
to help with estate planning and inheritance tax?

please put them in the comments below.
Thank you.
